label: Psychology
title: Why More Is Never Enough – The Hedonic Treadmill and the Art of Wanting What You Have
description: Why does the thing we wanted so badly become ordinary so quickly? Psychologists call it the hedonic treadmill. In this calm video essay we look at the famous lottery study, what later research revealed about adaptation, how Seneca and Epicurus described the same pattern two thousand years earlier – and three simple practices, rooted in both philosophy and psychology, that help you appreciate what you already have.

sections.text:
Think back to something you once wanted very badly. A phone, a job, an apartment, a relationship. Remember how certain you were that, once you had it, something inside you would finally settle.

And then you got it. For a while, it was wonderful. And then, almost without noticing, it became normal. The new phone became just a phone. The dream apartment became the place where you do the dishes. And your attention quietly moved on to the next thing.

Psychologists have a name for this. And philosophers were thinking about it more than two thousand years before them.

sections.heading: The Treadmill
sections.text:
In 1971, the psychologists Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell described what they called the hedonic treadmill. The word hedonic comes from the Greek word for pleasure. Their idea was simple, and a little unsettling. When our circumstances improve, we adapt. What once felt exciting becomes the new normal. And so, like someone walking on a treadmill, we keep moving, but we do not seem to get anywhere.

A few years later, in 1978, Brickman and his colleagues published a study that became famous. They interviewed people who had won large sums in the lottery, and compared them with people who had not. The lottery winners were not significantly happier than the comparison group. They also reported taking less pleasure in ordinary things, like talking with a friend, or hearing a funny joke.

The same study interviewed people who had recently been paralysed in accidents. They rated their current happiness lower than the comparison group, which is easy to understand. But the difference was smaller than most people would expect, and their ratings were still above the midpoint of the scale.

sections.heading: Not Quite a Law of Nature
sections.text:
It would be easy to turn this into a dramatic conclusion. Nothing matters. We always return to where we started. But later research has made the picture more careful, and more interesting.

In 2006, the psychologists Ed Diener, Richard Lucas and Christie Napa Scollon proposed a revision of the treadmill theory. Their work, and the studies that followed, showed that people do not all adapt in the same way, and not to everything. Long-term unemployment, for example, or the loss of a partner, can lower well-being for many years. Our baseline is not fixed in stone. It can shift.

So the treadmill is real, but it is not destiny. It is a tendency of the mind. And tendencies can be worked with.

What the research does suggest is this. We are surprisingly bad at predicting what will make us lastingly happier. We overestimate how much a new possession will change our lives, and we underestimate how quickly we will get used to it. The psychologists Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson have studied this under the name affective forecasting.

sections.heading: An Ancient Diagnosis

quote.lead: The Roman philosopher Seneca described the same pattern in a letter to his friend Lucilius.
quote.text: It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.
quote.author: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 2

sections.text:
Seneca was one of the richest men in Rome, so he knew what he was talking about. He noticed that wealth does not end wanting. Often, it does the opposite. Each new level of comfort quietly raises the bar for what feels like enough.

The Greek philosopher Epicurus, whose name today is wrongly linked with luxury, went further. He taught that a pleasant life depends on very little. Friendship. Simple food. Freedom from fear. Time to think. He distinguished between desires that are natural and necessary, desires that are natural but not necessary, and desires that are neither, like the craving for fame or endless wealth. That last kind, he warned, has no natural limit. And a desire with no limit can never be satisfied.

sections.heading: Wanting What You Have

quote.lead: One of his surviving sayings reads almost like an answer to the treadmill.
quote.text: Do not spoil what you have by desiring what you have not; remember that what you now have was once among the things you only hoped for.
quote.author: Epicurus, Vatican Sayings 35

sections.text:
What you now have was once among the things you only hoped for. This is not a call to stop wanting anything. It is a call to notice. The treadmill works silently. It turns gifts into background. Epicurus asks us to turn the background back into a gift.

Interestingly, modern psychology points in a similar direction. The researchers Kennon Sheldon and Sonja Lyubomirsky have argued that two things in particular slow down adaptation: appreciation, and variety. When we actively pay attention to something good, and when we keep experiencing it in fresh ways, the pleasure fades more slowly.

sections.heading: Three Ways to Step Off
sections.text:
So what can you actually do? Here are three small practices, each with roots in both philosophy and psychology.

The first is gratitude, but practised concretely. Not a vague feeling of being thankful, but writing down, now and then, a few specific things you would miss if they were gone. In a well-known study, the psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough asked people to keep a short weekly list of things they were grateful for. Compared with the other groups, they felt better about their lives as a whole.

The second practice comes from the Stoics, and it sounds strange at first. Today it is often called negative visualization. For a moment, imagine losing something you take for granted. Your health. Your home. A person you love. Not to make yourself anxious, but to see it clearly again. Seneca and Marcus Aurelius both wrote about versions of this practice. Often, the thing you imagined losing suddenly looks precious again.

The third is variety and savoring. Change small things. Walk a different way home. Eat slowly, and actually taste the food. Spend time, and not only money, on experiences you share with others. The treadmill feeds on habit. Attention slows it down.

sections.heading: Enough
sections.text:
The hedonic treadmill is not a flaw we can simply remove. In a way, it is part of what makes us resilient. The same mechanism that makes a new car feel ordinary also helps us recover from loss and disappointment.

But we do not have to run on it blindly. We can notice when the next thing starts to look like the answer to everything. We can remember the last time it wasn't. And we can turn our attention, again and again, back to what is already here.

Perhaps that is what it means to have enough. Not to have everything. But to finally see what you have.

short.title: Why the things you want stop making you happy
short.text:
Remember the thing you wanted most a few years ago? A phone, a job, an apartment. You got it. It was wonderful. And then it became normal.

Psychologists call this the hedonic treadmill. When life gets better, we adapt, and the bar quietly rises. In a famous study, lottery winners were not significantly happier than people who had never won.

More than two thousand years earlier, Epicurus offered a simple answer. Do not spoil what you have by desiring what you have not. What you have now was once something you only hoped for.

So take a moment today. Look at one thing you already have, and see it again.
